chunks: Vias in high-speed traces. The question: Should you put vias through high-speed traces?
A via is a small plated hole that carries a signal from one board layer to another. At slow speeds it acts like a plain wire.
For very fast edges it is a small bump in the path: a little inductance, a little capacitance and a leftover dead-end piece of barrel. That bump reflects part of the edge.
How much that matters depends on the edge speed.
Picture a smooth garden hose with one short kink and a dead-end side pipe. Slow water barely notices. A sudden splash hits the kink, and part of it bounces back.
The return current also has to change layers with the signal, so it needs its own path nearby.
The signal enters on L1, travels down the barrel to L3 and leaves. Everything below L3 (red shading) is an open stub.
The dashed square shows the anti-pad clearance in L2 (every plane the barrel passes has one); these clearances set the via's shunt capacitance.
The adjacent green ground via lets the return current move between the planes.
Via barrel: the plated tube between layers. It adds about 1 nanohenries of inductance (which resists fast changes in current) on a 1. 6 mm board.
Via stub: unused barrel left beyond the layer where the signal exits ("Via types and their tradeoffs"). Back-drilling: drilling out the stub from the far side of the board.
Return (ground) via: a ground via beside the signal via so the return current can follow.
Reflection: the part of an edge that bounces back where the impedance changes ("Reflections and why they matter").
Say a via adds 1 nanohenries in a 50 ohms line. The reflected fraction is roughly L over (2 Z 0 t r) . Here 1 nanohenries over 100 ohms equals 10 picoseconds.
For a 1 nanoseconds edge, 10 picoseconds / 1 nanoseconds is 1 percent. For a 100 picoseconds edge, it is 10 percent.
The same via is harmless on a slow bus and a real problem on a fast link. That is the whole idea.
"I avoid vias on fast signals where I can, because each one adds around 1 nanohenries of series inductance, a few tenths of a picofarad of shunt capacitance and a stub that resonates.
A 1 nanohenries via reflects about 1% of a 1 nanoseconds edge but about 10% of a 100 picoseconds edge, so it depends on edge rate.
When I must use one I keep the count low, put a ground via next to it for the return current, shorten or back-drill the stub, and make the two vias in a differential pair identical."
